Observing databases
" It must be the database! " Just like idx_11e7c252 blaming everything on the network, it's very common to
blame any type of problem on the database. Based on our experience, the database itself is
hardly ever the real problem. It's more common that the way an application accesses the
database is the root cause of bad performance or failures. Common examples include executing
too many individual database queries instead of leveraging the power of the database query
language (for example, SQL) to get data in bulk, or by executing inefficient queries that return
too much data that is not needed.
Observability best practice
Consult the documentation of your web and app servers. Java-based components
typically expose a lot of metrics through JMX. Chances are that there is also a
Prometheus exporter or support for OpenTel. If you use a commercial observability
agent, validate the out-of-the-box support for your version and target platform (Linux,
Windows, AIX, Solaris, etc.) of your servers! In all cases, you want to observe metrics
around throughput (number of requests), duration (response time of requests), service
failure rate, thread and request pool utilization, session counts, and CPU and memory
utilization.

" Full stack observability refers to a comprehensive approach to monitoring and understanding the
performance and health of an entire technology stack, from the end-user experience down to the
underlying infrastructure. It involves gathering and analyzing telemetry data (logs, metrics, traces)
across all layers of the stack to gain deep insights into system behavior and identify potential issues.
Essentially, it's about having a holistic view of your system, rather than relying on siloed monitoring."
(From Google's AI Bot on August 3, 2025, after providing the prompt "What is Full Stack
Observability?")
In the Observability and distributed systems section, we talked about using full stack
observability to answer key questions around the following:
Inventory: Which components are part of the system we are responsible for?
Dependencies: How are components connected and dependent on each other?
Interfaces/APIs: What are the boundaries of our distributed system to the consumers?
Health: Are all components working as expected or is there abnormal behavior?
SLA and root cause: Are end-to-end critical transactions experiencing issues, and
why?
Only when we have a holistic view of our systems, with high-quality and context-enriched
data from our end users all the way to the network or backend database systems, can we truly
claim that we have implemented observability the right way: the full stack way.
The observability goal is 100% coverage: start with production
infrastructure, then expand up and left
While it's not easy, it's important to aim for 100% coverage of observability. This doesn't mean
100% coverage of end-to-end distributed traces of every transaction, or capturing 100% of all
logs, events, or metrics of all your components. There is a lot of observability data that is
duplicated or too verbose. As an observability expert, it's about getting the correct 100%
coverage to answer the questions outlined earlier.
Many observability teams idx_9fddc2e9 start by rolling out basic infrastructure observability (hosts,
network, and processes) on the most critical parts of the system, which run the most critical
business applications. From there, you can expand up, left, and right in the stack:
Expanding up the stack: Move from network and infrastructure into application-level
observability. Once you know which applications and services are running on your
hosts, VMs, or pods, you can start capturing logs, metrics, and traces from those
components. Either enable your observability agent with deep insights or start
collecting Prometheus or OpenTel data.
Expanding into other systems: Move from your critical systems into adjacent systems

You will use exponential data growth as an opportunity!
As we build more complex distributed systems, we will see observability data growing

These decisions need to be based on high-quality and context-enriched data, as we have

Every organization will become a software company, and software will be a competitive
differentiator. Software, however, is not static and is not just introduced in production.
Software goes through the SDLC: from requirements, to development, through testing, into

Just as software goes through its life cycle, so must observability. Observability must not be an

Now that we've covered observability, we need to look at AI and the components required to
integrate observability with AI to achieve AIOps. While we expect that you already have some
understanding of AI, we're including this chapter both as a summary and to set context for
later chapters.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
Why AI is such a hot button topic and what is it good for right now

Choosing a language model
What can go wrong, and what you can do about it
Why AI projects are failing, and where they succeed

are recommended to follow along; however, they are not strictly required. These tools will be

Once you have your LLM running locally, let's dive in.
Why the hype around AI? What is AI good for?
AI isn't actually a new term, but has entered a new era with large language models (LLMs).
Systems such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude, and Gemini take in natural human language
instructions and return idx_81f0d3c0 a variety of outputs. This output could be images, code, music, or text.
The most important point is that what an LLM outputs is naturally understood by humans; it
needs no additional layers of translation to make sense.
This natural interface between computers and humans is exciting. It reduces the barrier to
entry for interfacing with machines. That doesn't mean you don't still need some level of skill
—prompt engineering is a key skill that we'll discuss more later in this chapter—but for a lot
of simple tasks, there's less mental overhead in interfacing with the machine.
AI versus automation
Before we had AI, we had already been using software automation for all kinds of tasks.
Automation is functionally turning human idx_abe7b550 knowledge into software that can execute a routine.
That routine can be as simple or complex as needed, with many common automation tools
having the ability to handle waiting on dependencies and race conditions. To write
automation, you must know how to successfully execute the tasks that the automation will be
taking over. Here is where AI has an advantage. When issuing an instruction to an AI agent or
assistant, you don't necessarily need to know how to do the task. The AI figures that out for

to AI instead of automation at all, but that wouldn't necessarily be the wisest move. When
evaluating AI, we must weigh what behavior will best support our use case. Consider two
practical archetypes—AI agents and assistants:
The agent (agentic AI):
Active: Can act independently

Both types have their strengths, but neither is a silver bullet. AI can be somewhat inexpensive,
but most automation systems are computationally trivial to run and therefore may cost more
to maintain than using AI for the same task.
Suppose we are responsible for a fleet of VMs in a cloud environment. Business logic says we
should run enough VMs to handle the workload quickly, but few enough to avoid wasting
money. Rather than hiring a large operations team—and risking burnout from repetitive tasks
—it is standard practice to rely idx_54e63952 on automation. It is relatively easy to configure alerts around
system capacity via observability tools such as Prometheus in Kubernetes environments or
CloudWatch for AWS-based environments. These alerts may indicate a need to scale up or
down, but only prompt human interaction; they do not replace a human. Since human labor is
pretty expensive, alerting or metrics around system capacity, such as CPU and memory usage,
are often paired with automation to respond to those alerts. In Kubernetes, this might involve
tools like the Cluster Autoscaler (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-
administration/node-autoscaling/#autoscalers) or KEDA (https://keda.sh/), also
known as Kubernetes-based Event-Driven Autoscaler, which integrate idx_5907cc7e with cloud
observability tools such as Amazon CloudWatch or Azure Monitor. For non-Kubernetes
environments, similar options exist, such as the Autoscale function in Azure Monitor. Alerts
and autoscaling rules are fine examples of automation that tend to be simple. When predefined
thresholds are reached, an alert is sent. When CPU and RAM utilization approach 100%, this
matches a pattern that once predicted crashes in old standalone servers. From there, your
automation rules may page an operator or add an additional VM. Whatever the action, it's
clearly defined in code, and the automation will never deviate from that definition. It has no
opportunity for intelligence that isn't codified.
Conversely, an AI agent could do the same thing and would be able to determine how to act
without strict definitions provided to it, but would cost more to run with very little value
added. However, if a system's scaling needs either follow a regular pattern or occur more
frequently than expected based on benchmarking, it may require further investigation.

Manual investigations into the cause of automated events can be somewhat tedious and time-
consuming for a human operator. Rarely does resource consumption happen all at once, so an
understanding of resource utilization may require analyzing data over a significant period of
time. An AI assistant provides immense value here, as it can help operators fetch, filter,
sanitize, annotate, and summarize information. It is unreasonable to expect operators to
review the last 5,000 events or combine 10 disparate data sources quickly, but these functions
are trivial for the assistant. Operational sophistication with AI can be taken one step further by
using the assistant to call the agent. The agent can then interpret operational data provided by
the assistant and act within the persona of a person responding to a ticket or page.
It is still reasonable, even if you're combining AI and automation, to expect automation rules to
page operators, even when the alerts are not actionable. However, it is also reasonable for the
AI assistant to identify patterns that can reduce the number of times an operational pager rings
at midnight. Unlike automation, which is limited by its programming, assistants can
essentially expand the resources available to a human operator, who may lack experience or
additional hands.
Between AI agents and idx_493bb3f0 sophisticated automation, there's a large intersection in the Venn
diagram of capabilities; the hardware needs are more significant for an AI agent. To run an
LLM-based AI toolset, you need a graphical processing unit (GPU), which can be idx_9d885c56 expensive
and potentially less readily available. So, why use AI agents instead of building and running
sophisticated automation systems? The difference comes down to ease of use and ease of
change. The ease of an AI agent is directly related to the unique value of AI as compared to
automation.
What is AI's unique value proposition?
AI can make seemingly intuitive leaps and is capable of unsupervised learning. It may respond
to prompts without the user understanding how it works, and without necessarily
understanding or caring about idx_d8a52106 the full context. Unlike earlier efforts designed to pass Turing
tests, this iteration has a duty to respond to changing inputs and conditions. This does not
mean Skynet-level intelligence (capable of tactically brilliant, fully autonomous decisions in
real time), but it does mean that within a session, an AI assistant can adapt to user needs, or an
agentic AI can start to detect patterns and make recommendations based on the information it
gathers.
Importantly, user interactions and inputs directly influence the outputs and behavior of the AI
agent or assistant as it changes to meet user expectations across various areas of demand. Let's

look at a simple use case that demonstrates the breadth of demand we're placing on our AI
systems: rubberducking. In software idx_b8ed3c4c engineering, the concept of rubberducking means
literally talking through something out loud to a rubber duck (or a small collection of them) to
help you think through and solve a problem. Generative AI is something beyond a rubber duck,

With agentic AI, the AI system will proactively review data and make recommendations or
even take action on what it thinks is needed without any human intervention. This effectively
gives an additional set of eyes and ears to the human team, allowing them to spend their time
on the work that AI can't necessarily do as well as a human, including training the AI systems.
What is AI good for (right now)
LLMs and what we call AI technologies today are fairly new, and in terms of availability,
they're basically brand new. In Chapter 3, we'll deep idx_bf1124b2 dive into several AIOps use cases and
practical examples, but we'll also consider a couple of use cases at a high level here, as these
examples will be helpful context for the rest of the theory covered in this chapter.
As discussed earlier, an agentic AI system connected to your monitoring and alerting stack can
act faster than a human. If a threshold is exceeded or an alert fires, the AI system can more
quickly gather and parse data, making it available as information for a human to consume,
which can include recommended actions or even directly taking action without human
intervention. As of now, most experts would not recommend blindly trusting the AI
recommendations. Just like you might with any human intervention, any actions, especially
write actions, should be reviewed by a human.
An AI system will also be quick idx_51f45167 to recognize and surface patterns. One example would be
identifying that there's a regular occurrence of resource pressure. This could be from
something such as a weekly backup job, normal user activity, or even due to a software bug.
While correctly identifying the root cause may not yet fall within the capabilities of the LLM,
identifying the pattern and making corresponding predictive scaling recommendations would.
This is superior to other autoscaling technologies because it is proactive, meaning the scaling
will occur before there is resource contention, as opposed to after a predefined threshold for
pressure has been hit.
As to root causes, AI can be used to quickly gather data, bubble up things that look notable
based on what you've asked it for, and help you identify a root cause faster, but it may not
necessarily be trusted to correctly identify the root cause of a complex issue.
47 The Elephant in the Room: Artificial Intelligence
A value-adding abstraction layer
In observability and operations, there's no one tool that solves all problems and provides all
the necessary business value. Trying to build idx_a497b443 and maintain such a tool would be a Sisyphean

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 46
chunks.content:
(from Sisyphus in Greek mythology) task. That's why most organizations will use multiple
related tools to get their entire observability and operational data. Once all that data exists,
turning the data into information can be incredibly challenging and takes a lot of dedicated
hours. For AIOps, this is the true power of adding an AI assistant or agent to the stack.
In a conversation with the authors, industry expert Premraj Varadharaj Singaravelu put it this
way: " [With AI] we are consolidating the observability data, not the tooling. The data should be tool-
agnostic."
Asking a computer to pattern match and gather data from multiple sources simultaneously has
been a key task for sysadmins and other operations professionals for decades. A simple Bash
script with some sed and awk commands can generate a report with sanitized data faster than
any human could hope to do by hand. Throwing an LLM at the same concept is even more
powerful.
Imagine you have a Kubernetes idx_09bb4d37 cluster running an internal developer platform (IDP) in the
cloud. Operational data may come from several sources, such as application data and metrics,
system runtime and metrics, the networking stack, a database, and so on. Tools such as
Prometheus and OpenTelemetry can help to gather real-time metrics from the runtime
environments, and most of that data is viewed not long after it is collected since it's often used
to determine deployment health or investigate an incident. However, the data that is collected
is often also stored long-term; data above a certain age threshold will likely be moved to cold
storage for cost savings. Retrieval of that data would require an additional process from this
second location. Additionally, logs may be collected and stored via something such as Loki,
which might store them in a third location, such as blob storage. Bringing together multiple
data types and locations is standard fare for most observability systems and the engineers
behind them. A good platform idx_1f33ba9e observability stack should be tool-agnostic, focusing instead on
practices and patterns that guarantee operational excellence.
In a different scenario, imagine you run a global financial system. When your user-facing
software has that much reach, it's often that customers take to social media to complain about
usability and performance issues. While traditional observability tools wouldn't necessarily be
able to bring this data into the operations team, an AI agent would be able to review social
media tags and compile that data alongside systems data. The addition of an AI tool removes
the need to consolidate or limit tools, as it becomes the interface by which the operations team
consolidates data. This application of AI also allows for that tool agnosticism we mentioned

sources if LLM is the interface. This allows for flexibility on the backend for teams building and
shipping applications to use whatever helps them be most successful in the operations
without jeopardizing the overall platform-level capabilities.
With all these moving parts and established practices around observability, how can you bring
things together to gain benefits from beyond a single LLM and its training data? How would an
AI agent know how to bring data from logs, social media, and metrics together? This is where a
Model Context Protocol server comes in.
Model Context Protocol
In software engineering, as problems become more complex, an abstraction layer or a layer of
indirection is often employed to address the complexity in a single place as opposed to in a
difficult-to-refactor sprawl across the idx_db9b0d14 code base. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is just
another example of this. MCP creates a standard that allows for a universal interface between
an LLM and other systems upon which it might depend, or it may need to act. The MCP could
be using an API or some other method for the interface, but that's unimportant to the LLM.
The protocol is exactly the same across every MCP server, allowing operators to seamlessly
integrate any number of purpose-built servers into their AI system.
MCP servers are purpose-built, meaning the abstraction they provide is for functionality that is
unique to the MCP. For this reason, an AI system is very likely to have multiple MCP servers at
play, allowing the LLM to consolidate data from multiple sources.
For example, in the case of our earlier scenario of computing resources rapidly approaching
100% utilization, you may have an agentic AI first check quota in the cloud for the creation of
another VM, and you may also have it check the applications running for evidence of a memory
leak. These are two basic tasks, but they require two totally different interfaces for the AI agent;
an MCP server would be leveraged for each.
An MCP server is a relatively easy-to-understand piece of software, but it's quite robust in its
capabilities.
The overall architecture follows the client-server architectural model, and the complete
component list of an MCP idx_23ea4b99 architecture, as specified at modelcontextprotocol.io, is as
follows:
MCP host: The AI application that coordinates idx_770000e0 and manages one or multiple MCP
clients
MCP client: A component idx_44ae76fc that maintains a connection to an MCP server and obtains
context from an MCP server for the MCP host to use
MCP server: A program that idx_f0a9c945 provides context to MCP clients

run, but more a piece of software that serves information (in this case, context) to another

connects to only one server. Since MCP is a standard, all components and features are also
standard across every implementation.
MCP server components and features
The MCP server is built of two components known as layers. The first is the data layer, and the
second is the transport layer. These are explained at length in the official MCP documentation
here: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture#layers.

Since the official documentation idx_770acbe4 will always be a better source of truth than a book, as it can be
regularly updated, we won't go into great detail here, but rather supply the current high-level
definitions as seen in the documentation:
Data layer: Defines the JSON-RPC-based protocol for idx_875d5d2b client-server communication,
including lifecycle management and core primitives, such as tools, resources, prompts,
and notifications
Transport layer: Defines the idx_c574b09c communication mechanisms and channels that enable
data exchange between clients and servers, including transport-specific connection
establishment, message framing, and authorization
In addition to the layers of the MCP servers, there are several primitives or fundamental
elements. The concept of primitives in MCP is the idx_1aa8ae3c real power of the standard. An MCP server
may use all primitives, or it could only use one. And each server supports Discovery, meaning
it will be able to list the primitives it supports on demand. This allows the LLM component to
learn about and leverage new MCP server capabilities without any need to program it to do so.
There are several MCP server primitives as defined in the official documentation for MCP at
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture#primitives:
Tools: Executable functions idx_d065eb42 that AI applications can invoke to perform actions (e.g., file
operations, API calls, and database queries).
Resources: Data sources that idx_f28dfe89 provide contextual information to AI applications (e.g.,
file contents, database records, and API responses).
Prompts: Reusable templates idx_50c4e4ee that help structure interactions with language models
(for example, system prompts and few-shot examples).
Sampling: Allows servers to request language model completions from the client's AI
application. This is useful when server authors want access to a language model, but
want to stay idx_a5a6303d model-independent and not include a language model SDK in their MCP
server. They can use the sampling/complete method to request a language model
completion from the client's AI application.
Elicitation: Allows servers to request additional information from users. This is useful
when server authors idx_7b4e751c want to get more information from the user or ask for
confirmation of an action. They can use the elicitation/request method to request
additional information from the user.

Later in the book, we will leverage MCP servers and show examples of them in action within an

system's knowledge with other industry methods, such as fine-tuning (which we will cover
more in Chapter 9). MCP servers are just another method of enhancing the capabilities of an AI

RAG versus CAG and how they relate to LLMs
Without additional components, the power of LLMs is limited by the data upon which they
were trained. However, their data can also be augmented with two additional natural language
processing approaches, which are standards in their own right.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and cache-augmented generation (CAG) are both
natural language processing approaches. However, their approaches to generating output are
different.
RAG versus CAG
While an LLM looks through idx_8347e488 the entirety of its knowledge base to idx_121dbcd8 determine what response to
generate, RAG and CAG both work with a more limited dataset to achieve response generation.
However, they are functionally different from each other and provide different advantages
based on the business case and data in question.
RAG is a reassuring way to mitigate the problem of outdated information. Suppose someone
falls comatose in Baltimore in 1982 and abruptly wakes in 1992. If they were then asked, " Who
is the president of the United States of America? ", they might answer " Ronald Reagan." They would
be incorrect, because their information would be 10 years out of date. If they could approach
the prompt like RAG, they would search for external sources about the current president and
consider the results along with the question. Like an LLM, this would allow them to provide a
correct response despite not having full context on the time period in which they've found
themselves.
From a business case perspective, RAG is the data augmentation of choice if your dataset is
very broad and/or changes very rapidly.

Chapter 2 52
In observability, if you asked " How is the system health today? ", an assistant with RAG
capabilities would check real-time metrics and logs before answering. The answer wouldn't be
immediate but would be highly accurate.
CAG offers an alternative: load a bunch of context and then respond. If the same person wakes
up and gathers information about the current state of the world, they can then answer
questions without external lookups. This allows them to also respond more quickly when
asked questions. In the case of computing, CAG is great for tightly scoped datasets with
infrequent updates, such as runbooks.
Using the same example, you would also include a log file: " Review these logs and tell me, how is
the system health today? " The answer you'd get would be nearly immediate, and it would also be
correct based on the logs. But if, in the minute between log retrieval and starting the session
with the AI assistant, the system crashed, the answer could be out of date.
However, if you had an AI agent troubleshooting idx_19888376 an alert, and the alert information along with
a runbook was supplied upfront, then the agent would be able to return the results of that
runbook execution very idx_abed508a quickly because the process of using that additional context was
already there.
There are pros and cons to both approaches. CAG has limits on how much data can be
referenced since it must all be placed in a cache upfront, but that data is available more quickly,
so any prompts that rely on the cached data will return results faster than they would with
RAG.
RAG is less limiting because, while the process of doing the lookup adds additional time to the
response, the data can be in real time, which would be useful for understanding software
health or the current state of an application by parsing the observability metrics.
While RAG and CAG systems can stand on their own, that would be a very atypical use case for
them, as they're often used as an augmentation to an LLM, bringing in newer or external data
to the model beyond its training data. RAG and CAG are both also different from fine-tuning,
which is a specific method of adding new data to an LLM's training data. Unlike RAG and CAG,
where the augmenting data remains distinct, fine-tuning allows users of AI systems to extend
the system's knowledge into a specific domain of expertise, especially against data that is
proprietary.
For all three types of generation (LLM, RAG, and CAG), the data relied upon can be indexed and
weighted to help the AI system provide a more accurate response. This is an important aspect
of ensuring quality in an AIOps system, as it's a protective measure against errors and failures.
53 The Elephant in the Room: Artificial Intelligence
Choosing a language model
Did you know that there are technically idx_eb462207 two flavors of language models? As well as LLMs, there

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 52
chunks.content:
idx_55991975 are also small language models (SLMs). SLMs are architecturally similar to LLMs; however,
they are trained on a significantly smaller amount of data, making them often more efficient
and less costly to run, but increasing their likelihood of hallucination or errors. This can be
mitigated via fine-tuning, which is the process of further training your language model, but if
the prompt falls outside the scope of the training data of the model, the response is very likely
to be inaccurate. SLMs may also be more prone to bias because the data in their sampling may
be more biased, either intentionally or unintentionally. Bias has no special meaning here; it is
the same as bias within humans, just transferred to the AI via training data.
Whereas an LLM having more data makes it a very general-purpose tool, an SLM, properly
tuned, is a purpose-built tool designed to be excellent at the one application for which it's been
trained. But not all LLMs or SLMs are the same size.
DeepSeek, which features heavily in this chapter, comes in multiple sizes. The larger the size,
the more knowledge it has. LLM knowledge comes not just in the total amount of data, but
also in parameters. Parameters are the characterization of the data. Just as you should label
your observability data, training data used to train a language model will have weights, biases,
annotations, and other characteristics. Parameters are used not just during training, but also
during fine-tuning. See Chapter 9 for more on how to fine-tune.
However, throwing the largest size model at a task that does not need that level of reasoning is
likely not going to show performance gains as opposed to using the smaller model with its
capabilities expanded for the idx_13aec5b7 domain.
Additionally, DeepSeek, Claude, Gemma, and other LLMs come in variants that are specifically
designed for distinct purposes. DeepSeek, Gemma, and Claude all have models specifically
designed as coding assistants, for example. Despite being smaller models, when used for their
designated purposes, these models will outperform the larger models.
However, model size and purpose aren't the only data points to consider during model
selection. Aside from the size of the model, the model's context length will also impact
accuracy and performance. Context length is measured in tokens and is the total number of
tokens the language model can have stored per session. On your computer, this will be stored
in the random access memory (RAM) used by the idx_7694b041 model. In other words, the model's context
is what it can and will remember within the session, and the length is the measurement of how
much context you can expect to use.
A token is a block of data, typically around four characters long. Larger context length means
more data/tokens. When you input a prompt, it's chopped up into tokens, and the response

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 54
chunks.content:
Chapter 2 54
starts as tokens that the model assembles and emits. Many AI vendors charge based on token
consumption, so in other words, when you're paying for tokens in AI systems, you're paying for
the data transfer. We'll cover cost management of tokens more in Chapter 9; for now, we'll
continue with the importance of tokens for accuracy.
For this chapter, we used the DeepSeek-R1 model, which has a context length of 128,000
tokens. This DeepSeek model will tell you, if you ask, that that is approximately 64 pages of
text or a few hours of conversation. As your session with an AI system continues and the token
count goes up, if you exceed the context length, you will find that the system begins to become
less accurate. It may forget a critical piece of information, or it may hallucinate an answer that
seems plausible, but isn't accurate.
When selecting a model, it's important to understand some information about the training
data used within the model, including whether the model was designed to excel in a specific
area and what limitations, including context length, the model has. Once you have that
information, map your use cases and system design options to select one or multiple models.
For example, choose an SLM for code reviews, but an LLM for operational data parsing. It's also
important to have an idea of the volume of data you have to ensure your model will match your
needs. The good news is that all the connectors, hosting, and so on are the hardest things to
achieve in an AI system. Swapping one model for another can be very easy.
You might choose to swap a idx_b481989b model if you're noticing high error rates or poor accuracy. Next,
we'll look into what can go wrong in your AI systems and what options you have for doing
something about it.
What can and will go wrong (and what you can do
about it)
While AI is a powerful tool in our toolbox, just like any other software, it is susceptible to
errors, bugs, or other issues. The idx_ca963973 following is a semi-exhaustive list of the types of problems an
operator of an AI system may notice.
Incorrect user expectations
Early in the chapter, we mentioned that the benefit of AI is that it feels like magic. This can,
however, lead to inaccurate expectations. Users of any AI system that is implemented should
have a clear understanding of what the system will reasonably be able to do and know.
Otherwise, the AI assistant or agent may give incorrect answers or recommendations, or even
take dangerous actions.
55 The Elephant in the Room: Artificial Intelligence
Users and operators of AI systems need to know the following:
How current the training model data is
What capabilities the AIOps system has
What a good prompt looks like
Known limitations
Known limitations are the largest umbrella, as an AIOps implementation is a very purpose-

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 54
chunks.content:
built system. As a purpose-built system, what it's expected to do and not to do should be very
clearly defined. Users should be informed about the places where the model is expected not to
be leveraged so they do not attempt to stretch the model beyond its intended purpose.
Additionally, in a new implementation, you may not yet have significant system data to fine-
tune the model against. If there are gaps in training data or tuning data, call out the areas
where those gaps are so that users may be aware that the model could lack accuracy for those
tasks at this time. This gap in data could result in inference-related errors where the LLM does
not have enough information to correctly interpret the prompt. Inference, in an LLM, is
somewhat complex, but ultimately, it is based on tokens in and out. The LLM considers the
prompt and what it's already begun to respond with as it continues to generate its response
token by token. If there are not enough parameters or related data to contextualize the prompt,
the response is more likely to be error-prone. This is why it's important to highlight to new
users and operators what the AIOps system does and doesn't know yet. And while setting user
expectations correctly will not prevent all issues or errors, setting up your operations team for
success is a key aspect of a successful use of AIOps.
Hallucination and errors
Hallucination in LLMs is defined by the AI responding to a prompt with information that is not
just wrong, but not rooted in any idx_08b7ab8a data from its dataset. An LLM can often idx_f54f01db hallucinate in the
form of identifying patterns that are non-existent, or inventing information that doesn't exist
within its cited source.
A hallucination is different from a simple error, although both can be problematic.
Let's take this example of Gemma being asked to count the number of times the letter i appears
in the word Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis (the correct answer is six):

ChatGPT worked a little better, which was expected as it is a newer and larger model than the

Reasoning errors and hallucinations can be a frustrating experience, especially when an AI
system sounds convincing and may be accessing data you can't easily verify, making it easy to
be misled. Here are some recommendations to reduce the chances of these errors:
Choose a model that meets your expectations. Larger models have more reference data
and may be idx_511bdbe1 more accurate. Smaller models will be fast and highly accurate when
queried against their training data, but are more likely to hallucinate or make errors
when prompted for answers outside the domain of their training data.
Rely on tried-and-true aggregation tools such as OTel and Prometheus, and use your
AIOps to interpret from there.
Fine-tune your model with domain-specific expertise. We will cover how to fine-tune
further in Chapter 9.
Consider augmenting with RAG or CAG systems to improve model accuracy.
Connect to an MCP that extends the model functionality into the domain of expertise
your organization cares about.
Data poisoning
Data poisoning is when the data that an LLM has been asked to interpret is deliberately
incorrect. Large organizations with global reputations may rely on scraping social media as

chunks.heading: Chapter 2 58

part of their overall observability idx_9e17e99f strategy. Unfortunately, users sometimes notice issues faster
than automation or even AI. However, social media or other sources of data where there are
humans creating input could be subjected to data poisoning.
This IBM blog (https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/data-poisoning) gives a very good
overview of the types of data poisoning and cites specific examples from within the industry.

The prompts used for this example are intentionally suboptimal to ensure that the
errors occurred.

Chapter 2 60
Their examples focus primarily on intentional poisoning, and we'll cover that and more
security-related topics later in Chapter 9. What we'd like to raise in this chapter is the fact that
in many systems, data poisoning need not be deliberately malicious in order to have negative
outcomes.
Let's look, for example, at the label-flipping attack. Labeling observability data is a common
tool used to help create semantically correct traces and aggregate relevant application data in
distributed systems. However, label flipping on the observability data could easily happen via
human error or via an application team deciding to change their labeling without necessarily
informing the operations team. This can cause the data that the team asks the AI agent for to
be mistakenly categorized as not present, or make it so that the data shown doesn't match
expectations and understanding. That can further spiral into lengthy debugging sessions
against the AI agent, which would ultimately reveal that it worked as intended, but the data
was poisoned.
In another scenario for data poisoning, consider an AI agent that sends updates to Slack about
potential system outages based on chats or tickets from users. Many operations teams with
customer-facing ticketing systems will often get tickets that are opened where the users claim
the service is broken. A discerning idx_10105887 human can ask the right questions to further identify what, if
anything, is broken, or whether a user error is at play. However, an AI agent may not
necessarily know how to ask idx_067076ee the correct questions or interpret the answers. Therefore, it may
not correctly identify user error or a problem in a dependency, and could declare an outage
where one does not exist.
Catastrophic forgetting
Catastrophic forgetting or catastrophic inference is probably the most self-explanatory of the
possible things that can go idx_713ed389 wrong with an AI. This occurs when a model is trained on new data
or new tasks, and subsequently forgets its previous knowledge. This can happen as a result of
retraining or fine-tuning. It's our assumption that you are likely not spinning up entirely
custom models from scratch, but are instead relying on vendors of LLMs. The techniques for
preventing and mitigating this are pretty deep into the weeds of how AI and neural networks
work, so we'll consider them out of scope for this work, but we recommend this whitepaper
from Cornell University if you're interested in this topic: https://arxiv.org/abs/
2501.01045#.
What is important for engineers who are setting up AIOps systems is how to identify
symptoms of catastrophic forgetting. Catastrophic forgetting can be identified by measuring
the performance of systems that rely on the AI agent. This is where observing your AI is very

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 60
chunks.content:
critical: monitoring response times, overall system health, and identifying whether routine AI
tasks are suddenly taking much longer than the norm. While latency or AI errors are not only
61 The Elephant in the Room: Artificial Intelligence
caused by catastrophic forgetting, they are also a hallmark of it and should be looked for via
automation and other traditional observability practices.
Infinite loops
An infinite loop is pretty much exactly idx_4731660e what you would expect. The LLM gets stuck infinitely
going through the same series of steps and ultimately needs to be canceled by the user.
Take this example of DeepSeek getting stuck trying to work through the prompt " How many
times does the letter R appear in the word strawberry? ":

Prompt engineering helps
Prompt engineering is functionally the process of identifying the best way to ask an LLM
system for output in order to get idx_81b938c7 consistent results. In Prompt Engineering for Generative AI by
James Phoenix and Mike Taylor, the authors lay out the five principles of a good prompt:
Give direction
Specify format
Provide examples
Evaluate quality
Divide labor
This practice and the methods of being successful are critical skills for any team looking to
build and leverage AI systems. If we look at the earlier examples of infinite loops, we see that
while initially the LLM struggled, after the prompt was improved, it was successful in
completing the task. A different language model may be able to successfully answer the
original prompt as written, but it's important to know how to successfully interface with the
model you're using day to day.
You do not need to struggle with idx_f8ef253c prompts or trial and error them endlessly. When you have an
AI model, the best expert for its utilization is already at your fingertips. AI knows how to be
successful with AI. Where your team may not have as much experience, the AI agent does
know what to do and how to idx_ce6e96ef do it.

Why do AI projects fail, and how can you succeed?
AI projects can fail for idx_c65849a0 several reasons, none of which are unique to AI specifically:
Scope unclear or too large
Cost
Lack of expertise
Insufficient or slow ROI
Too many bespoke implementations
The number one strategy we recommend for helping to ensure the success of your AIOps
project is to adopt a product mindset. Projects end, whereas products evolve; by taking a
product mindset into your creation idx_f2579b64 of an AIOps implementation, you can map a path to a
successful product via milestones, key performance indicators (KPIs), and other benchmarks
to measure success.
A purpose is the vision; it sets what you seek to achieve. Any project is unlikely to succeed
without clarity of purpose, substance, and success criteria. For emerging and poorly
understood technologies, doubly so. A quick, if not painless, litmus test of your purpose is to

whether the project is too loosely defined or tries to do too much. This does not mean the
project is too ambitious, just that the scope needs refinement. The risk of being on the bleeding
edge of technical advancements is that it's easy to fall into the trap of a solution looking for a
problem or trying to tackle all the world's problems at once. Those are the projects that will
fail, so identify the problems you have early, and how you will know whether they are solved.
A good product has a clearly defined purpose, a set of principles to guide it, and starts as a
minimal viable product (MVP). Principles idx_11b7fbc1 are the guardrails against which you weigh

Your principles may be technical limitations, business ethics, security and compliance
requirements, or business goals. These idx_1769f6cb should function as the laws you cannot violate in order
for your product to be successful.
In project management, principles can be represented as requirements, but also as KPIs. KPIs
are not one-and-done metrics of success, but rather are continuously evaluated. As you add
features and functionality to a project, your KPI metrics must continue to reflect success, or the
KPI may need to be re-evaluated. An example KPI would be Our database backups are restorable
within 15 minutes, which would need to be validated every so often (quarterly, monthly, etc.) to
determine whether it's being met or not. If it's not being met, say, because database size and
complexity have grown, then the KPI idx_a42ce2ab could be adjusted, or the process improved to match.
These can seem similar to objectives and key results (OKRs), and they can be used with or
independently of each other. However, an OKR is different because it is a time-bound objective.
Like KPIs, OKRs should be measurable; the objective may not be as measurable, but the key
results should be easily quantified with data. The key results are how you will seek to achieve
the objective you've set.
It's okay for an OKR to be very big picture and a KPI to be more focused. These tools are
intended for different aspects of business and product management. As long as your OKRs and
KPIs can be measured objectively, you're doing it right.
In addition to being helpful for shaping the technical roadmap, OKRs and KPIs are useful
communication tools. How does the CEO know that the AI project is doing great things?
Especially for AIOps projects, which will largely be internal-facing and not as obviously
revenue-impacting, it's important to set and communicate the business value of what you're

Lack of expertise will be a challenge as these technologies are new and rapidly evolving.
Reading texts such as this one is a great start, and you will find a Further reading section at the

By approaching your AIOps implementation as a product, you can keep track of costs and

For more information on how to approach an initiative like this with a product mindset, we
recommend Platform Engineering for Architects, another Packt title, written by Max Körbächer,

Summary
In summary, AI as we define it today is an evolving space where the technology is still seeking a
level of stability that we find in older machine learning technologies. It has some strengths and
weaknesses, and requires human input and data tuning to be successful at tasks. However,
with engineers guiding and defining the use of AI within an organization and applying a
product mindset to its governance, AI projects for operations can be a powerful tool for the
modern organization. In the next chapter, we'll dive further into the use cases AIOps can solve

" How do we set up 10,000 custom Service-Level Objective (SLO) alerts for our critical Tier 1 API
endpoints? How do I create dashboards for my top 100 applications? " Those are common questions
that we hear from engineers and application owners. Those questions come up when they try
to apply the same monitoring mindset, they used 10–20 years ago: handcrafting dashboards
and custom alerts for a small number of critical systems. But the world has changed. This
approach is not scalable in today's ever-growing dynamic hybrid cloud infrastructure, with
new applications, services, and features being developed, deployed, and released daily.
In this chapter, you will learn why we, the authors, would respond to these questions with: " I
understand where this requirement comes from! You are responsible for ensuring the health,
availability, and resiliency of your digital services as they are business-critical. As your architecture has
evolved over time, so must your approach to monitoring. Let us show you an easier, scalable way to
achieve your requirement by leveraging cloud-native approaches to observability and AI! "
We are building on the foundation we covered in the previous two chapters: how observability
has evolved from monitoring and how the recent advancements in AI can help us better
manage and understand the explosion of observability data. We will discuss how these two
technologies combined can improve the day-to-day challenges faced by IT operations, SREs,
application owners, and business owners in ensuring that the digital services they are
responsible for are running as expected.

When data on glass and static alerts fail
" We used to have 1,000 dashboards. Now we are down to 50! " is how a successful observability
transformation story idx_054d426c ends. It's a transformation where data was previously placed on many
dashboards, but it was not actionable. If the same can be achieved with a more focused

" Can our monitoring tool set 10,000 custom thresholds? " is a question we have heard more than
once. The answer is, " Yes! But why do you have this requirement? Where does it come from? "
Static thresholds were great on static infrastructure. When having three database production
servers, five applications, and two web servers, it made sense to set static thresholds on CPU,
memory, Garbage Collection (GC), worker idx_c0817912 threads, and connection pool utilization. IT
operators knew those machines well. They probably gave them easy-to-remember names, such
as sql-prod-1, app-frontend-4, or ws-lb-2. Traffic to those applications hosted on those servers
was predictable and stable. Therefore, setting static thresholds was a good solution to get
alerted if one of those servers wasn't as healthy as it was supposed to be.

Fast forward to 2026: instead of three database production servers, we have several different
database cloud services—some used for storing records, some acting as caches, and others just
as a data lake. Instead of application servers that run monolithic Java applications, we have
something between 100 and 500 Pods running across various Kubernetes clusters. The number
of running Pods changes depending on event-driven and load-driven scaling, which is why it's
hard to pinpoint a specific number at any given moment. And the web servers? Most of them
have been replaced with load-balancing services, Ingress controllers, or API gateways. The
architecture has changed quite a bit! But when it comes to monitoring, we often see the old
mindset and approach simply being applied to modern architecture. This is where the
requirement of " Can our monitoring tool set 10,000 custom thresholds? " comes from. Instead of a
handful of neatly idx_93e37586 named servers, we now have thousands of components. If you still want to
get alerted to every CPU spike or GC activity, that's when you really need to set 10,000 custom
thresholds. But that's neither practical nor necessary.

Alternatives to static alerts on infrastructure metrics
The curious mind idx_c7dc6699 will probably have the following questions: " Why do you say we do not need
those alerts anymore? Don't we have CPU, memory, or GC that we need to keep healthy? "
The answer is " Yes, we still rely on CPU, memory, disk, network, and more! But orchestration layers
such as Kubernetes or cloud service providers take care of providing the right amount of CPU, memory,
and disk based on the current required load. This eliminates a lot of the need for static thresholds as we
leverage elastic infrastructure and automated orchestration to provide exactly the right amount of
compute, memory, and storage that is needed to ensure we can deliver on our SLO."
You may now think: " Wait a minute, that seems like really bad advice! We could quickly end up in a
situation where our systems just keep scaling up, potentially endlessly, without any governance and
cost control! " You are spot on again! Hence, we need to clarify where we still need static
thresholds, where we don't, and where we have new ways to get alerted or scale.

Well-defined critical system boundaries, such idx_6401accc as API rate limits
Known limits in runtimes or design, such as worker threads or queue lengths

Beyond CPU and memory: cloud-native golden signals
CPU, memory, disk, and idx_a8c050e1 network have always been great metrics to get alerted on, or as a
trigger for infrastructure scaling. Expanding on that, many site reliability teams follow the
Google SRE handbook's definition of the " four golden signals " (latency, traffic, errors, and
saturation). SRE and ITOps teams, therefore, typically know the limits of their system very well
and can take corrective actions to remediate the situation, for example, resizing a virtual
machine to meet current memory and CPU demand, restarting a rogue or hanging process that
stopped handling requests, or distributing incoming load across multiple virtual machines
behind a load balancer to ensure faster individual response times.
Modern cloud-native architectures, especially container orchestrators such as Kubernetes,
introduced new components, layers, and built-in automation that automate or simplify those
tasks. The Kubernetes operator pattern, for instance, with its built-in control loop, automates
some of those tasks that ITOps teams had to implement themselves, changing the focus for the

ITOps teams:
Automated restarts of hung processes: Kubernetes takes care of restarting unhealthy
Pods for us. Alerting, therefore, shouldn't necessarily be on unresponsive Pods, but
more when certain Pods get restarted very frequently, when restarts start having issues,
or if they impact other components.

Automated resizing and scaling of Pods: Kubernetes can resize (vertical scaling) or
deploy more instances of (horizontal scaling) Pods based on changed resource
requirements or a change in workloads. Alerting, therefore, must focus on detecting
when those resizing and scaling tasks are running into issues or cause service
disruptions.
Automated scaling of clusters: Like any system, Kubernetes is limited to the amount
of CPU, memory, and disk of all its nodes. Cluster autoscaling, however, can provision
new nodes from the underlying infrastructure virtualization. Alerting, therefore, must
focus on whether scaling of the cluster itself works as expected, and whether it finishes
in a timely manner to avoid any disruption of the Pods that are deployed.
With some of the automation moving into the various layers of our cloud-native platform
(Kubernetes, OpenShift, or managed cloud services), we need to focus on the new health
indicators and then decide how to best alert on them and which ones to use for scaling
decisions.
When it comes to cloud native, we—the authors—feel it's time to redefine the golden signals
that help us monitor health and get alerted on and scale every layer of our dynamic stack. The

infrastructure layer (bottom) to idx_dbac8161 the application layer (top), as well as the observability layer
(across).
Resource layer
Without a doubt, we need idx_42ab6e7f sufficient resources to handle idx_f28bfe64 all workload requests. Doing proper
testing and capacity planning and then setting up alerting and scaling based on compute,
storage, and memory doesn't change all that much.
In cloud-native architectures, we see more components that communicate via various
channels. More than ever, network latency, throughput, and quality of service play a critical
role in overall stability and performance.
Orchestration layer
Kubernetes is the idx_89994060 leading container orchestration idx_515d9f3f layer and provides a lot of important health
indicators. If you are not using Kubernetes, then your orchestration layer of choice
(homegrown or an offering from a vendor) will have similar indicators that allow measuring
health. Key indicators are around the availability of the orchestration layer API as well as how
fast the orchestration layer can fulfill requests to schedule and deploy new workloads.

We recommend baselining Ingress and Egress traffic volume. A significant spike or drop

Workload layer
A workload is a set idx_cb1ec250 of Pods and containers that run an idx_c04d2a64 application or a service on a Kubernetes
cluster. It defines the Pods and containers, how they should be deployed, how they are sized,
and how they communicate.
The most important thing is that workloads can be started in a timely manner, keep running,
or restart successfully when needed. Keeping an eye on Pod failure rates, the reasons why they
fail (for example, running into limits), and the number of failed restart attempts is essential.
Cloud-native observability tip for Kubernetes
We recommend baselining the scheduling latency and deployment latency of new
workloads. That's the time it takes from kubectl apply until Kubernetes finds the
proper node to deploy it, and how long it then takes until the Pod is deployed. An
increase in pending Pods will ultimately lead to slower deployments and is an indicator
that your clusters are not healthy or don't have enough resources to fulfill all those
incoming schedule and deployment requests.
Tip

On top of that, we recommend baselining the time it takes to start a workload and how
long workloads are running. The startup time depends greatly on the type of workload.
A database-like workload will most likely take much longer to start and run much
longer than a small microservice that is only needed for certain use cases and otherwise
spun down. Init containers or dependencies, on the other hand, can also impact small
workloads. We therefore recommend baselining the workload start time and workload
lifetime by the type of workload. Any change in timing behavior deserves to be looked
at more closely!

Platform service layer
Platform idx_0abf05f4 services idx_1a106c3b are typically shared services that are used by business services and
applications. Examples of those are message queues, service meshes, databases, and other
storage services, as well as critical shared business services such as an authentication service
or Single Sign-On (SSO). All of these services provide some type of API to their consumers
and, therefore, we see that the four golden signals (latency, throughput, errors, and saturation)
are used to monitor and alert on health.

We recommend baselining key health indicators of queues, such as wait time, queue
length, message sizes, compression, and processing time. A queue that keeps growing
or where wait time increases over a period of time is a warning signal that needs to be
addressed to avoid impacting dependent services. As most critical services also have

Service layer
With services, we mean all idx_7a3839ff business services that power the idx_0c33fa4a applications that run on your
platform. For a financial services organization, those might be services such as account-
service, trading-service, transfer-service, or currency-service.
SLOs around availability, performance, and failure rate for those services are a good idea as
they give a good indication of whether the services are delivering on their promise. While SLOs
and their error budgets and burndown rate are great tools, they also come with management
and operational costs when not done right, hence the following tip!
Application layer
Most services provide idx_12c11124 critical APIs for business applications idx_f912aa12 and their critical business
transactions. Examples are the number of users that are logged in to their online banking
system, creating a new bank account, or transferring money between accounts.
For any organization, this is the most critical layer, as this is where your business generates
revenue or where you enable your employees to do their job!
At a high level, you want to make sure that those systems and critical transactions are
available. At a minimum, we suggest using synthetic tests to validate that those key
transactions work from end to end and then alert on any availability or performance
degradations.
Cloud-native observability tip on SLOs
Too often, we have seen organizations define SLOs for every single internal and external
API endpoint of every service. That results in thousands of SLOs without any consistent
thresholds across the organization. A better approach is to define SLOs only for end
consumer APIs along the critical path of your business transactions. Even then, it's best
practice to provide templates for gold, silver, and bronze or tier 1, tier 2, and tier 3 APIs
with predefined company-wide standards on thresholds and alerts. For all other APIs,
we suggest using anomaly detection and then seeing whether the idx_e41815fc anomaly of an
internal API is really impacting the upstream idx_a48c3d10 SLO. More on that topic later in this
chapter, in the From ops to business: SLO-based impact analysis section.
Tip

Observability layer
There is a idx_b65e4653 saying: the best comes last. No alerting or scaling idx_952023e7 would be possible if we didn't have
any observability data. Therefore, it's important that we also apply the same health principles
to the observability stack. This includes the health of the instrumentation, collection, storage,
and analysis. When using OpenTelemetry, for example, we need to make sure that all collectors
are properly sized, all receivers are healthy, no data is dropped, and all observability signals are

forwarded to the backend analytics platform.
Cloud-native observability tip on business
We also suggest baselining key indicators on whether your business is healthy. That
includes the number of concurrent active users on your system, the throughput of
business processes and transactions, how long critical transactions take, and the
number of transactions per user or session. If those numbers start to deviate from
normal behavior during a regular day or work week, then you should act. Focusing on
the business impact has become key in modern observability, which is why we cover
this in more detail later in this chapter in the From ops to business: SLO-based impact
analysis section.
Tip
Cloud-native observability tip for your observability stack
Besides following the best practices around self-monitoring of your observability
tooling, we suggest baselining the received, processed, and ingested volume of all your
observability signals. The baseline will show you whether you have a sudden spike or
drop in observability data. Root causes could be misconfiguration or an unexpected
change in manual or automated instrumentation. We have seen examples where the
number of spans increased 100x because of a coding mistake using manual
instrumentation.
A key indicator where a static threshold can be used is the percentage of dropped
signals, as ideally, you don't have any dropped signals unless it's intentional.
The time until analysis indicator defines how long it takes from data collection until
that data point is available to be charted in a dashboard or available for alerting. The
longer this time, the more reactive rather than proactive your responses to issues will
be.

These discussed indicators and metrics should give you a good starting point when it comes to
understanding the health of your cloud-native platform. As not everyone runs on Kubernetes,
OpenShift, or other container orchestration platforms, it's important to understand the layers
of your specific idx_50923142 environment. Make sure to consult the idx_d9929b36 best practices documentation of the
vendors you use. A great additional and recommended way to choose the right metrics is by
conducting some load and performance tests.
Choosing the right metrics through proper load testing
Every application idx_962b6ed0 and distributed system is unique. Therefore, it's not possible to provide a
golden rule template that includes all metrics one should keep an eye on. While the metrics we
discussed previously will be important for most systems, it's important to understand the
characteristics and dynamic behavior of your system under different conditions.
Load and performance testing is a key practice that helps you understand the dynamic
behavior of your application. It allows you to identify the critical components in your
architecture, for example, which queues or shared services are causing ripple effects when they
start slowing down or failing, or what the expected maximum throughput a critical
component can handle is before it starts breaking.
Going into all of the relevant details about setting up proper load testing is beyond the scope of
this book. We do, however, want to give you some guidance on what the key steps are and give
you pointers on where to find more information.
Step 1: setting up a test environment
We could stop right here if you can test in production. For very bold people, that means you don't
do any upfront testing at all and just deploy and react to whatever happens. For those who are
less adventurous, it may mean using the failover production environment for load testing.
Some organizations also use the live production system during low traffic times. Both scenarios
depend heavily on how your production environment is set up and whether it's possible to
deploy a different version of your software in those environments. For those who can't do that,
please keep reading.
Ideally, test environments reflect production environments as closely as possible. This,
however, is not always possible due to the costs of running those large systems and the time it
takes to set up and operate such a system. While standing up the required infrastructure for a
short period of time has gotten easier, thanks to automation and on-demand available cloud
resources, it's most often very challenging to replicate production-like datasets of your systems
of records.
There is plenty of material available online about how to overcome some of these challenges,

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 84
chunks.content:
such as generating representative production data without running into any compliance issues
or even considering mocking or simulating those data layers.
85 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
If a production-like system is not achievable, we suggest setting up a scaled-down version that
you can stand up idx_0fd37ec8 and operate within acceptable costs, because it helps you understand which
indicators across your layers are leading indicators for problems at scale. And remember, that's
really what this exercise is all about.
Step 2: defining realistic scenarios
When testing a sports car, you would not just test it by driving in first gear at 20 miles per
hour. That would not reflect how the car will be used by a real driver. The same is true for
software testing. Before creating any test scenarios, you need to understand what the top real
end user scenarios are. Ideally, you would get this information from the owners of the
applications and services you are testing. Also, ideally, you would simply look into your
observability stack and extract this information from there; for example, what are the top hit
APIs, or what are the most common click sequences in your web UI or API call chains? Also, you
can get a sense of how this load is distributed across those scenarios and in the course of a
regular 24-hour day. These are all insights that allow you to best model your load test to be as
close as possible to production.
Once you have this, you can pick your load-testing tool of choice and create your test scenarios.
There is no shortage of available tools, including lots of open source options, such as JMeter,
Gatling, k6, and Locust. Pick the one that works best for you and allows you to easily create and
maintain your test scenarios.
Step 3: expand-left observability
The term shift left has been used quite a bit over the past years. Typically, this means that we
shift tasks and responsibilities earlier idx_990e158e in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). A
better term for our case is expand left because what we really want to do is expand the usage of
tools and practices from production earlier into the life cycle. For testing, this means we simply
use the same observability tools and practices for our load-testing environment. This not only
allows us to capture relevant data to identify our critical indicators for production monitoring
but also allows us to validate that our observability setup works as expected. For example, are
you capturing all your logs, metrics, and traces? Can you access them in the way you expect to
in production? Does your observability setup alert you on bottlenecks during your load testing
automatically because you have set up some dynamic baselines or use machine learning to
identify anomalies?

Step 4: running tests
Ideally, you would idx_32ccaf8b run your tests continuously, kind of like simulating production load all the
time. This allows you to continuously validate that your test system can be run. It also allows
you to identify how the system behaves under continuous load. For example, this approach is
great to identify any memory or connection leaks that only materialize after a certain time. If
you have such a setup, you can also validate how a running system behaves under load when
you deploy a new version of a component while it's still under load. That's a great test as this is
what will happen in production when you have to roll out a new change.
Now, if such a continuous test is not possible, then we suggest running shorter tests at a
regular cadence, maybe once a day or a couple of times per week. This provides continuous
feedback to your engineers and gives you continuous insights into how changes affect the
internal behavior of the system.
There are also different types of tests with different load behaviors, such as increased load,
steady load, spike tests, and stress testing. You can find more information about different
simulated behaviors and their goal in many online resources. You can also apply chaos testing,
where you simulate failures throughout the load test to bring the system into a critical
situation, for example, artificially slowing down a network connection, killing Pods, or turning
off a critical service such as your database.
All of these tests and the simulated chaos should give you plenty of observability data to
analyze and identify new technical indicators that you can apply to your production
monitoring and alerting. This brings us to the next step.
Step 5: identifying critical indicators
Load tests fulfill several purposes. On one side, they tell us whether the system behaves as
expected under the simulated load. On the other side, they allow us to optimize system
parameters and configuration to optimize the system's output under load, for example,
tweaking our connection pool sizes or adapting resource and request limits on our containers
for optimal resource usage. It also allows us to validate that our observability captures all the
data we need to identify problems, performance bottlenecks, and their root causes. This gives
us more confidence that, once we deploy in production, we can also find those root causes if
there is an issue in production that we need to fix. If we didn't find any indication of an issue
when we should have, then it means we need to think about what additional metrics, logs, or
traces we need our developers to put into their system for better insights!
The other benefit is that we can look at all the data collected after the test is finished and see
whether there are certain metrics, logs, or traces that contain information that serves as early

chunks.heading: Chapter 3 86
chunks.content:
warning indicators of a performance or availability problem that was uncovered during the
test.
87 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Once you have those indicators, make sure to monitor them in production as well. Use them as
early warning health indicators, as we discussed earlier in this chapter. Also remember that as
systems constantly change with every release, you want to continuously validate and update
those critical indicators as they may change over time.
Now you should understand that modern observability is about looking beyond CPU, memory,
and disk. While those metrics still play an important role, we have new indicators of system
health, for example, how fast a Kubernetes cluster can deploy Pods. We also discussed that
setting and maintaining static thresholds for alerting doesn't scale when we have to deal with
thousands of cloud-native components compared to traditional architectures. There are simple
and sophisticated baselining algorithms that modern observability platforms provide as an
alternative idx_4278d2b0 that automatically adjust their alerting based on historic behavior.
To conclude this section, let's look at a specific implementation scenario from one of the
organizations we have worked with.
Use case: baseline alerting on Kubernetes health
There are various idx_836c9cb4 ways to define the health of a system, and the same is true for Kubernetes.
One method to observe health is to look into how well and successfully Kubernetes provisions
the requested resources. The nature of Kubernetes is that it retries failed attempts, thanks to its
implementation of the controller and operator pattern. Therefore, just alerting on a failure is
not a good thing because the system will retry upon failure. A better way is to analyze trends
and alert on abnormal behavior. This is where a baseline is a perfect fit. The following
screenshot shows using a baseline on the number of Kubernetes Provisioning Failed events.
When we ingest these events, we can baseline what "normal" looks like and then alert on
"abnormal" or "out of baseline" situations, as shown in the following graph:

static thresholds
The preceding graph shows that at 7:00 a.m., there was an unusually high number of
provisioning failed events. Using a static threshold would potentially lead to too many false

positives, as we can see that there are constant failed events happening. Using a baseline here
also means our alerting will automatically adjust if the "base error events" decrease or increase
over time. What we are really after is abnormal, out-of-baseline behavior.
Now that we have seen practical cases of how to elevate monitoring from static threshold
alerting on well-known infrastructure metrics to leveraging baselining across the different
layers of a modern platform, it's time to think about how we can fundamentally change the
approach to observability.
We need to move idx_4d300aca from trying to understand a system once it's running in production toward
having software engineering teams including observability as a key software requirement
before even starting to write a line of code.
Observability-driven development
" Here is the new software package from development. Now, you in operations take it and figure out
how to run it in a stable way." This is the classical " throw it over the DevOps wall " mentality that
many idx_6d3a69da organizations applied in the past.
We can debate whether the term shift left or expand left is a better description for embedding
observability as a requirement earlier in the software development process. We, the authors,
prefer the term observability-driven development because it describes the mental shift that
needs to happen within an organization to treat observability as a software requirement.
Similar to test-driven development, which idx_5c142136 focuses on creating tests before writing the
business code, observability-driven development focuses on defining what and how to observe
software before it gets deployed for the first time in a testing or production environment.
Transformations such as this don't happen overnight or because somebody mandates it. As
with many other transformations, it has proven successful to start idx_3f9e74ac with a lighthouse project
that executes on the new way of embedding observability in the development process. If that
project succeeds, others will follow. Let us walk you through the key ideas and steps for such a
lighthouse project's implementation.
Step 1: defining internal and external system health
indicators
When you look at your idx_05acaea3 mobile phone and see the battery charge turning from green to yellow
and eventually red, you know that you must act quickly, otherwise your phone will die. The
same is true when driving a car and the dashboard shows the engine's heat moving toward the
red zone. This means the engine is moving to an unhealthy state that could result in
unrepairable damage. The root cause can be bad driving, such as putting the motor in constant
high RPMs, or it could be a leakage of cooling water.

chunks.content:
Just like those simple health indicators, we need to define how to measure the health of our
software systems and components. We typically start with measuring health from how the
system is perceived by the caller or consumer of the system. When the system is called through
an API, we can follow the best practices around the four golden signals:
Throughput: Can our system process the number of requests per time interval that we
designed it for?
Latency: Can our system finish processing the request in a time acceptable to our end
users?
Errors: Is our system returning valid responses for valid inputs most of the time?
Saturation: Is our system using the expected resources based on our capacity
planning?
But as with our example of the car engine overheating, we must define additional technical
leading indicators to get alerted before the system becomes unhealthy for the user. We need to
define metrics that give us an early warning signal and can also be used for root cause analysis.
Here are examples:
Cache hit ratio: For systems that have internal caches, this metric is a great indicator
of whether the cache works as expected or needs an update before it impacts overall
performance and stability.
GC: For memory churn-intensive systems, GC runs and GC time are good internal
health indicators. A change in behavior suggests that there might be some memory
leak, or that the memory behavior has changed, which may require adjustment to heap
sizes or GC strategies.
Incorrect request format: For any request/response systems, it's important not to
waste too much time on incoming messages that have an incorrect format. It's typically
a sign of wrong usage by the caller or could also indicate some type of denial-of-service
attack. Knowing the percentage of incoming request messages that are invalid by
nature can be a good health indicator as it allows us to react to the problem before it
impacts the processing of correct messages.
Once we know what good external and internal health indicators are, we need to make sure
these indicators can be measured.
