Step 2: defining how to measure health indicators
For most health indicators, there might already be an existing way to extract them from logs,
metrics, or traces. The response time of an API, for example, is something we can measure by
enabling a Prometheus exporter on the Ingress controller or extracting it from the HTTP
request logs. If none is available, developers can export additional data using Prometheus or
OpenTelemetry, or write it as a log that can then be converted into a metric in the data
pipeline, for example, through the OpenTelemetry Collector. When using an agent-based
observability approach, chances are high that you get those metrics out of the box without any
additional development involvement.
For system-specific internal indicators, such as incorrect request format or roundtrips to the
database, or any business indicators, such as number of opened bank accounts, it will be necessary
to define how to measure idx_447b62ae them and how to expose this information to the observability tool
(Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, logs, and so on). You also need to specify what value ranges of
those metrics indicate healthy or unhealthy; otherwise, nobody would take action if those
indicators fall outside the expected value range.
Step 3: providing easy access to this data for engineering
Capture everything, everywhere, and make it easily accessible! This is the only way observability-
driven development has a chance to become adopted as it avoids an additional step for
engineers to find the data they are looking for.
For this to work, we need to answer two critical questions.
Where was the data captured, and who needs it?
Later in this chapter, in the Context is king: the quality of observability data section, we will dive
deeper into how we can enrich observability when it gets captured with all this additional
metadata. This metadata is needed to answer the following question.
Where and when does this data need to be made available, and
to whom?
First, we need to learn which tools our engineers use on a day-to-day basis and where they
spend most of their time for certain tasks:
Which IDP is used for self-service, for example, Backstage, Kratix, or Confluence?
Which IDE is used for coding, for example, Visual Studio Code or IntelliJ?
Which Git platform is used for commits, for example, GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket?

Discord?
Which ticketing system is used for task management, for example, Jira or ServiceNow?
Next, we need to analyze what decisions engineers need to make in these tools for which tasks
and how observability data can help. For example, when troubleshooting problems, would

for team standup
Most development idx_84074bdc teams have daily standups to discuss their daily tasks and get advice from

more context. This enables many new use cases, such as those already discussed earlier, for

Let's dive into the details!
Context is king: the quality of observability data
We've said it before and idx_c3c35d33 we'll say it again: observability data is growing and will continue to do so!
The challenge is how to deal with that growth and ensure that it provides valuable insights,
rather than just letting it sit in a big lake of data that accumulates costs for storage.
We know that we need the help of AI to manage this data, but AI can only help us if the data is
of the right quality and is enriched with enough context about where it comes from, how it
relates to other data, and which part of the data is needed for decision-making.
We will walk through best practices around how and where to enrich data and the use cases
where this enriched data enables us to get more value out of our observability implementation.
Let's start with the challenge of scale and the need for semantic conventions.
From pets to cattle: semantics for observability
If you have managed idx_2de8f376 infrastructure before, you have probably heard about the pets versus cattle
analogy. Instead of treating every server like a unique, cared-for pet with a lovely name and
even a remembered birthday, we need to think about infrastructure more like cattle. Cattle
thinking means idx_651158a1 that we have a potentially unlimited number of components that we treat as
disposable and replaceable when problems occur. For that to scale, we also need to think about
automating tasks versus manually taking care of every individual component.
In cloud-native architectures, there are no pet names by default. But there are certain semantic
conventions when naming entities. Objects in Kubernetes, for instance, get a new Unique
Identifier (UID) when idx_2076e07e the resource gets created and a generated name that will be different
for every new object instance even though the object may have been created before. Take a Pod
as an example. If you create a workload with the name my-critical-svc, then every Pod for
that workload (can be a single replica or multiple) will have a unique name, such as my-
critical-svc-1694 and my-critical-svc-4352, whenever the Pod gets restarted or scaled up.
This also means that in observability, we need to adjust the way we think about monitored
entities: a host, cluster, node, workload, Pod, service, serverless function, or database. All of
these entities might no longer just have a unique name throughout their lifetime, especially
when they are restarted, scaled up, or scaled down. Gone are the days of creating a dashboard
for servers named Joe, Sally, and Hugo. Instead, we now create dashboards that are specific to
certain use cases and idx_045cf6f8 tech stacks, which can then be filtered based on agreed-upon metadata
with standardized semantics. This metadata can be extracted from labels, annotations, or tags
